concepts.title: Running a Statistical Project: The Full Pipeline

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Running a Statistical Project: The Full Pipeline' refers to.
questions.a: This chapter assembles the whole course into a student project: choose a topic, set objectives, design the questionnaire, collect data, organise and present it, apply statistical tools -- percentages, averages, index numbers, correlation -- and end with conclusions and bibliography.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Running a Statistical Project: The Full Pipeline'.
questions.a: The project is the course in miniature -- one question carried through every statistical stage to a conclusion.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Running a Statistical Project: The Full Pipeline' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.1 (source: kest108.txt project sections (steps of a project, choosing a topic or objective, designing questionnaire, conclusion and bibliography))

concepts.title: Applying the Tools: Percentages, Averages and Correlation

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Applying the Tools: Percentages, Averages and Correlation' refers to.
questions.a: On the collected data the student applies the year's toolkit: percentages for composition, mean, median and mode for central tendency, index numbers for change over time and correlation for relationships -- choosing the tool that fits the question rather than using all of them blindly.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Applying the Tools: Percentages, Averages and Correlation'.
questions.a: Right tool for the right question -- composition asks percentages, centrality asks averages, relationships ask correlation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Applying the Tools: Percentages, Averages and Correlation' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.2 (source: kest108.txt application sections (percentage calculations, averages, index numbers, correlation in project analysis, interpretation of results))

concepts.title: Organising, Presenting and Interpreting Project Data

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Organising, Presenting and Interpreting Project Data' refers to.
questions.a: Once collected, project data must be classified into a frequency distribution, presented in tables and diagrams, and then interpreted: what the figures mean for the objective, what patterns emerged, and what limitations qualify the conclusions.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Organising, Presenting and Interpreting Project Data'.
questions.a: Collect is only halfway -- classify, display and interpret turn data into a project's findings.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Organising, Presenting and Interpreting Project Data' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: 1.3 (source: kest108.txt organisation sections (classification of collected data, tabular and diagrammatic presentation, interpretation of results, limitations of the study))
